To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified two genes which are markedly upregulated during dehydration of a nematode and that the proteins they encode are highly hydrophilic, unstructured, and able to protect proteins from aggregation during drying.

we have identified a novel, dehydration-inducible protein, anhydrin, and that we have shown that the nematode Group 3 LEAp LEA protein is processed during desiccation into smaller polypeptides which retain their activity.

(1) a hydrophilic, natively unstructured, nematode protein, Anhydrin, is induced during dehydration and is able to bind and stabilise other proteins; (2) an LEA protein is processed into smaller polypeptides during dehydration, with the smaller forms also able to bind and protect other proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the molecular basis of invertebrate desiccation tolerance and the mechanisms of dehydration-induced gene expression, with the aim of identifying molecules which may be of practical value in agriculture and medicine.
identifying and characterising dehydration-inducible proteins in invertebrate anhydriotes, with the aim of understanding the molecular basis of desiccation survival.
the identification and functional analysis of genes and their proteins which are implicated in invertebrate anhydribiosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

anhydrobiotic invertebrates, like plants, have evolved a range of strategies to cope with desiccation, including the induction of hydrophilic proteins, but that the molecular mechanisms of desiccation survival in invertebrates may differ in detail from those in plants.
the molecular basis of anhydrobiosis is not well understood, but is likely to involve the action of hydrophilic proteins, including those that are processed into smaller forms.
anhydrin and LEA-like proteins may play a major role as stabilising agents during dehydration and rehydration, but that their precise roles in invertebrate anhydrous are not yet clear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are at the beginning of understanding how anhydrobiosis is regulated at the molecular level, and that we are beginning to understand that there is no single mechanism of anhydrobiosis but rather a variety of strategies, some of which are shared between different organisms and others of which are unique.
we are beginning to identify a range of dehydration-responsive proteins which are likely to be important in the acquisition of anhydrobiosis by nematodes.
anhydrobiosis involves the induction of a range of hydrophilic proteins, some of which are novel, others of which have counterparts in other organisms, including plants.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the hydrophilic proteins of invertebrates are not just the equivalent of plant LEA proteins but may have evolved to be more effective in their role of protecting proteins from desiccation-induced damage.
the molecular mechanisms underlying anhydrobiosis are likely to be highly conserved, at least in terms of the proteins that are involved.
, in nematodes as well as plants, the acquisition of desicca-tion tolerance involves the induction of a suite of dehydration-responsive genes, many of which are involved in protein stabilisation.
